scenes.visual: Dark slate background (#0F172A). Along the upper third, a warm slate-blue plasma membrane bilayer (#60A5FA) ripples gently with embedded teal receptors (#2DD4BF) whose tails point down into the dark navy cytosol. Centered in large clean white type (size 48): 'Pulled In, Sorted Back Out'. Subtle ambient drift in the extracellular fluid above.

scenes.tts: A macrophage swallows the equivalent of its whole surface about every half hour, yet it never shrinks. Where do all that membrane and its receptors go? Pulling plasma membrane inward as vesicles is called endocytosis.
scenes.caption: A macrophage swallows the equivalent of its whole surface about every half hour, yet it never shrinks. Where do all that membrane and its receptors go? Pulling plasma membrane inward as vesicles is called endocytosis.
scenes.visual: Title fades out smoothly. The same plasma membrane bilayer (#60A5FA) expands to fill the upper 60% of the frame, schematic label 'Plasma membrane' (size 30, white) and 'Cytosol' below. Repeated small membrane patches dimple inward and pinch off as vesicles carrying teal receptors (#2DD4BF) downward while the overall membrane length holds steady. On the upper right, a clean animated question banner fades in: 'Where do they go?' (schematic).
scenes.narration: A macrophage swallows the equivalent of its whole surface about every half hour, yet it never shrinks. Where do all that membrane and its receptors go? Pulling plasma membrane inward as vesicles is called endocytosis.

scenes.tts: Each minute, a macrophage pulls in about three percent of its surface. Total area divided by uptake rate gives turnover time. One hundred percent divided by three percent per minute equals about thirty three minutes. Membrane must return just as fast.
scenes.caption: Each minute, a macrophage pulls in about 3% of its surface. Total area divided by uptake rate gives turnover time. 100% ÷ 3%/min ≈ 33 minutes. Membrane must return just as fast.
scenes.visual: Keep the animated plasma membrane above; in the lower half, build a clean computed turnover gauge synchronized to each spoken number: first '3% / min' highlights as vesicles bud off; then the formula '100% ÷ 3%/min' slides in (size 34, crisp white); finally '≈ 33 min' illuminates in bright teal (#2DD4BF) as a circular progress ring fills to 100%. Return arrows rise back toward the membrane as the last sentence plays.
scenes.narration: Each minute, a macrophage pulls in about 3% of its surface. Total area divided by uptake rate gives turnover time. 100% ÷ 3%/min ≈ 33 minutes. Membrane must return just as fast.

scenes.tts: Receptors ride inside with that membrane, starting at a coated pit. A curved lattice called clathrin shapes the pit, yet clathrin touches neither membrane nor receptor. Adaptor proteins bridge them, gripping a membrane lipid, a receptor tail sequence, and clathrin.
scenes.caption: Receptors ride inside with that membrane, starting at a coated pit. A curved lattice called clathrin shapes the pit, yet clathrin touches neither membrane nor receptor. Adaptor proteins bridge them, gripping a membrane lipid, a receptor tail sequence, and clathrin.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto one section of the same slate-blue plasma membrane (#60A5FA, schematic). A teal receptor (#2DD4BF) carrying a white-gold ligand (#FDE68A) on the outer face has its cytoplasmic tail extending down into the cytosol. Amber adaptor blocks (#F59E0B, label 'Adaptor') snap onto a highlighted lipid patch on the inner leaflet and onto the receptor tail. Coral-orange three-legged clathrin units (#FB923C, label 'Clathrin') then attach to the adaptors—never touching membrane or receptor directly—and pull the membrane into a curving cup.
scenes.narration: Receptors ride inside with that membrane, starting at a coated pit. A curved lattice called clathrin shapes the pit, yet clathrin touches neither membrane nor receptor. Adaptor proteins bridge them, gripping a membrane lipid, a receptor tail sequence, and clathrin.

scenes.tts: The pit deepens until it hangs by a thin neck. A large G T P splitting enzyme called dynamin wraps a collar around that neck. Hydrolyzing G T P tightens the collar, cutting the neck to free a vesicle.
scenes.caption: The pit deepens until it hangs by a thin neck. A large GTP-splitting enzyme called dynamin wraps a collar around that neck. Hydrolyzing GTP tightens the collar, cutting the neck to free a vesicle.
scenes.visual: Continuous motion from s03: the coral-orange clathrin-coated cup deepens until only a narrow slate-blue neck joins it to the plasma membrane. Bright violet rings (#A78BFA, label 'Dynamin') assemble into a tight helical collar around the neck. A brief crisp flash labelled 'GTP → GDP' triggers the collar to constrict; the neck snaps cleanly, and the coated vesicle drifts downward into the cytosol.
scenes.narration: The pit deepens until it hangs by a thin neck. A large GTP-splitting enzyme called dynamin wraps a collar around that neck. Hydrolyzing GTP tightens the collar, cutting the neck to free a vesicle.

scenes.tts: The clathrin coat strips off, and the bare vesicle fuses with the early endosome. A small switch protein called Rab five marks this sorting station. Because the membrane folded inward, the receptor's cytoplasmic tail still points into the cytosol.
scenes.caption: The clathrin coat strips off, and the bare vesicle fuses with the early endosome. A small switch protein called Rab5 marks this sorting station. Because the membrane folded inward, the receptor's cytoplasmic tail still points into the cytosol.
scenes.visual: Coral-orange clathrin and amber adaptors peel away and fade as the bare slate-blue vesicle drops to meet a large round compartment filling 60% of the frame height below: the early endosome, rimmed with electric cyan Rab5 markers (#38BDF8, label 'Rab5 early endosome', schematic). The vesicle merges smoothly into the endosome wall. A glowing arrow traces the teal receptor: its white-gold ligand sits inside the lumen, while its cytoplasmic tail clearly protrudes outward into the cytosol (label 'Tail in cytosol').
scenes.narration: The clathrin coat strips off, and the bare vesicle fuses with the early endosome. A small switch protein called Rab5 marks this sorting station. Because the membrane folded inward, the receptor's cytoplasmic tail still points into the cytosol.

scenes.tts: Two physical features sort cargo here. First, proton pumps acidify the inside to about p H six to six point five. Many ligands, including L D L, let go in that mild acid. Second, thin tubes sprout from the round body.
scenes.caption: Two physical features sort cargo here. First, proton pumps acidify the inside to about pH 6 to 6.5. Many ligands, including LDL, let go in that mild acid. Second, thin tubes sprout from the round body.
scenes.visual: On the same Rab5 early endosome: small pump blocks on the membrane push H+ icons inward, shifting the lumen colour smoothly from pale blue-grey (pH 7) to soft amber with badge 'pH 6–6.5'. As the amber tint settles, the white-gold LDL particles (#FDE68A) detach from the teal receptors (#2DD4BF) and float freely in the round central lumen. Simultaneously, two narrow slate-blue tubules grow outward from the upper sides of the round endosome body.
scenes.narration: Two physical features sort cargo here. First, proton pumps acidify the inside to about pH 6 to 6.5. Many ligands, including LDL, let go in that mild acid. Second, thin tubes sprout from the round body.

scenes.tts: Geometry separates membrane from fluid. Surface over volume is three over the radius for a sphere, but two over the radius for a tube. Give the tube one tenth the sphere's radius: two over one tenth is twenty, against three. That is nearly seven times more membrane per unit of fluid, so freed ligands stay mostly in the body.
scenes.caption: Geometry separates membrane from fluid. Surface ÷ volume is 3/R for a sphere, but 2/r for a tube. Give the tube one-tenth the sphere's radius: 2 ÷ 0.1 = 20, against 3. That is nearly 7× more membrane per unit of fluid, so freed ligands stay mostly in the body.
scenes.visual: Beside the early endosome, a clean computed inset compares a wide circle ('Sphere: surface ÷ volume = 3/R') with a narrow cylinder ('Tube: 2/r'). Each step appears as it is spoken, in crisp white and teal: 'r = R/10', then '2 ÷ 0.1 = 20 vs 3', then '≈ 6.7× membrane per volume'. Meanwhile, in the live endosome beside it, freed white-gold LDL particles drift mainly inside the spacious amber round body while the thin tubules remain mostly membrane.
scenes.narration: Geometry separates membrane from fluid. Surface ÷ volume is 3/R for a sphere, but 2/r for a tube. Give the tube one-tenth the sphere's radius: 2 ÷ 0.1 = 20, against 3. That is nearly 7× more membrane per unit of fluid, so freed ligands stay mostly in the body.

scenes.tts: Now make a prediction. This receptor carries no tag, no mark telling the cell to destroy it, and its ligand has let go. Does it stay in the round body, or ride a thin tube back out?
scenes.caption: Now make a prediction. This receptor carries no tag, no mark telling the cell to destroy it, and its ligand has let go. Does it stay in the round body, or ride a thin tube back out?
scenes.visual: Inset fades out. Camera centers on the amber Rab5 early endosome with a highlighted untagged teal receptor (#2DD4BF, label 'No tag') drifting near the junction between the round body and a thin sprouting tubule. Two dashed arrows point one into the body and one up the tubule. A clean high-contrast question card appears at the bottom: 'Round body or thin tube back out?'
scenes.narration: Now make a prediction. This receptor carries no tag, no mark telling the cell to destroy it, and its ligand has let go. Does it stay in the round body, or ride a thin tube back out?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card 'Round body or thin tube back out?' on screen. Keep slow ambient motion: freed white-gold ligands drift gently in the amber round body, the untagged teal receptor hovers and oscillates gently near the tubule mouth, and a subtle thin progress bar ticks across the bottom.

scenes.tts: It rides a thin tube back out. No tag is needed, because the tubes hold most of the membrane, so a wandering receptor usually drifts into one. Fast tubes marked by Rab four return receptors in minutes. A slower route using Rab four and Rab eleven takes tens of minutes.
scenes.caption: It rides a thin tube back out. No tag is needed, because the tubes hold most of the membrane, so a wandering receptor usually drifts into one. Fast tubes marked by Rab4 return receptors in minutes. A slower route using Rab4 and Rab11 takes tens of minutes.
scenes.visual: Question card fades; the tubule arrow illuminates in bright mint-teal (#5EEAD4). The untagged teal receptors glide into the sprouting tubules while freed white-gold ligands remain in the amber round body. One short mint-teal tubule labelled 'Rab4 (fast: minutes)' pinches off and fuses directly back with the plasma membrane above; a second path labelled 'Rab4 / Rab11 (slow: tens of min)' loops through a small pale recycling compartment before rising to the surface (schematic).
scenes.narration: It rides a thin tube back out. No tag is needed, because the tubes hold most of the membrane, so a wandering receptor usually drifts into one. Fast tubes marked by Rab4 return receptors in minutes. A slower route using Rab4 and Rab11 takes tens of minutes.

scenes.tts: An L D L receptor repeats that round trip roughly every ten minutes. Some cargo heads to the Golgi instead. Otherwise, early endosomes sort internalized receptors, returning untagged ones to the surface.
scenes.caption: An LDL receptor repeats that round trip roughly every 10 minutes. Some cargo heads to the Golgi instead. Otherwise, early endosomes sort internalized receptors, returning untagged ones to the surface.
scenes.visual: Pull back to show the full continuous cycle in one world: coated pit entry → Rab5 early endosome → ligand release in amber lumen → mint-teal recycling tubule returning empty teal receptors to the slate-blue plasma membrane, with subtle badge '~10 min cycle' beside the returning LDL receptor. Motion slows gracefully as the background dims.
scenes.narration: An LDL receptor repeats that round trip roughly every 10 minutes. Some cargo heads to the Golgi instead. Otherwise, early endosomes sort internalized receptors, returning untagged ones to the surface.

scenes.visual: Clean dark slate end card (#0F172A) with one centered line only (size 40, crisp white, no subtitle or secondary text): 'Early endosomes sort internalized receptors, returning untagged ones to the surface.'
